metadata.title: Female students and students from more affluent families benefit more from fear of failure in learning achievements: A study based on 77 economies

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 student microdata across 77 economies and filters to students with complete fear-of-failure items, ESCS (SES), and achievement scores. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, and the analysis is conducted via multilevel structural equation modelling in Mplus rather than design-based ML estimation. Because the paper does not specify a weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or replicate method (e.g., BRR/jackknife), readers should treat the estimates as model-based associations rather than fully design-weighted population inferences. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and, if available in the released files, replicate weights to obtain design-correct uncertainty estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 across all 77 economies, restricting to students with non-missing values for ESCS (SES), all items of the fear-of-failure scale, and achievement scores in mathematics, reading, and science. Cases with complete missing values on any of these components were excluded; the authors report dropping students with missing values on all fear-of-failure items, achievement in mathematics/reading/science, and SES. After this exclusion, missingness remained only for 33 cases in SES, which were imputed using SPSS 26 regression imputation prior to further analysis.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (77 economies) Mathematics achievement (single plausible value)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ML-SEM Model 1 fit: RMSEA=0.021, SRMR(within)=0.015, CFI=0.999, TLI=0.997. Model 2 justification: ΔG2=1516.81 (df=6), p<.001. Fear of failure main effect: β=0.05 (90% CI [0.046, 0.055], p<.001). SES main effect: β=0.38 (90% CI [0.374, 0.384], p<.001). Gender main effect: β=0.08 (90% CI [0.066, 0.084], p<.001). SES×Fear interaction: β=0.01 (95% CI [0.004, 0.008], p<.001). Gender×Fear interaction: β=-0.08 (95% CI [-0.087, -0.073], p<.001). Moderation effect sizes: SES f2=0.0001; Gender f2=0.006.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data across 77 economies, the study leveraged fear of failure, socioeconomic status (ESCS), and gender to model mathematics achievement (single plausible value), finding that fear of failure was positively associated with mathematics achievement and that SES positively moderated this relationship while gender negatively moderated it. This indicates that strengthening supportive, equity-oriented responses to students’ fear of failure may yield larger achievement benefits for students from more advantaged backgrounds and for females, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (77 economies) Reading achievement (single plausible value)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ML-SEM Model 1 fit: RMSEA=0.021, SRMR(within)=0.015, CFI=0.999, TLI=0.997. Model 2 justification: ΔG2=1516.81 (df=6), p<.001. Fear of failure main effect: β=0.07 (90% CI [0.060, 0.068], p<.001). SES main effect: β=0.37 (90% CI [0.364, 0.374], p<.001). Gender main effect: β=-0.24 (90% CI [-0.248, -0.231], p<.001). SES×Fear interaction: β=0.02 (95% CI [0.016, 0.020], p<.001). Gender×Fear interaction: β=-0.09 (95% CI [-0.097, -0.085], p<.001). Moderation effect sizes: SES f2=0.004; Gender f2=0.008.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data across 77 economies, the study leveraged fear of failure, socioeconomic status (ESCS), and gender to model reading achievement (single plausible value), finding that fear of failure was positively associated with reading achievement and that SES positively moderated this relationship while gender negatively moderated it. This indicates that interventions addressing fear of failure may be particularly beneficial for students from higher-SES families and for females in reading, while the reported moderation sizes suggest effects that are statistically meaningful but not necessarily large.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (77 economies) Science achievement (single plausible value)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ML-SEM Model 1 fit: RMSEA=0.021, SRMR(within)=0.015, CFI=0.999, TLI=0.997. Model 2 justification: ΔG2=1516.81 (df=6), p<.001. Fear of failure main effect: β=0.06 (90% CI [0.056, 0.065], p<.001). SES main effect: β=0.37 (95% CI [0.360, 0.370], p<.001). Gender main effect: β=0.003 (90% CI [-0.006, 0.011], p=.631). SES×Fear interaction: β=0.01 (95% CI [0.012, 0.016], p<.001). Gender×Fear interaction: β=-0.09 (95% CI [-0.093, -0.081], p<.001). Moderation effect sizes: SES f2=0.0001; Gender f2=0.008.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data across 77 economies, the study leveraged fear of failure, socioeconomic status (ESCS), and gender to model science achievement (single plausible value), finding that fear of failure was positively associated with science achievement and that SES positively moderated this relationship while gender negatively moderated it. This indicates that science instruction and student-support policies that channel fear of failure into persistence may show stronger achievement associations for females and for higher-SES students, though causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional multilevel SEM framework.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-sectional study uses PISA 2018 student microdata from 77 economies to examine whether fear of failure predicts achievement in reading, mathematics, and science, and whether socioeconomic status (ESCS) and gender moderate these relationships. Achievement is modeled using PISA plausible values, with the authors using only the first plausible value per domain, and fear of failure is measured via three 4-point items (ST183Q01 and ST183Q02 items). The analysis is multilevel structural equation modelling (ML-SEM) with latent interactions (LMS) estimated in Mplus, reporting strong model fit for the baseline model (e.g., RMSEA=0.021, CFI=0.999, TLI=0.997) and significant improvement when adding interactions (ΔG2/df=252.80, p<.001). Fear of failure shows positive associations with all three achievements (β≈0.05–0.07, p<.001), while SES strengthens these effects and gender suppresses them (gender×fear interactions negative, p<.001). Limitations include the absence of explicit design-weight usage reporting and the inability to establish causal effects from cross-sectional data.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper is indexed under machine learning themes, the reported methodology is multilevel structural equation modelling with latent moderated structural equations (LMS) rather than predictive ML algorithms. Consequently, no ML learners (e.g., Random Forest/XGBoost) are evaluated, so ml_techniques is left empty. The study still provides empirical, model-based associations and moderation effects using PISA 2018 plausible values, which are captured in main_findings.
